title: Close for Survival: The Sales Training I Give My Team
summary: The full sales training Yousif runs for his closers and setters. Why it's never the leads, why selling is a numbers game, why you sell the outcome and not the tech, and how to drop a prospect's guard by being willing to walk away.
content:
Yousif Alias has been closing deals since he was 17. He named this training "Close for Survival" after the stretch when every call mattered: close the deal, or go back to being a dental assistant with $35,000 of debt. This episode is the full training he runs for his own closers and setters, recorded on Zoom and cut down to the parts that teach something.

Sell the outcome, never the system

When Yousif sells voice AI, he doesn't walk a prospect through features. The owner of a roofing company doesn't care how the agent is prompted. He cares about fewer missed calls, more booked appointments and more customers. Every sentence on the call should point at that result.

His comparison is a doctor visit. Your back hurts, the doctor hands you the medicine, and nobody explains the chemistry. "Find the problem. Give them the price." He calls it ditching the pitch. The script he gives his team is a framework, and on his own calls he just talks to people the way he'd talk to anyone, which takes the nerves out of it for both sides.

"It's never the leads"

One setter books five to ten appointments a day. Another makes the same dials and books one. Same leads, same offer. The difference is how they approach the person on the other end. When sales dry up, Yousif's first move is to check the follow-up, before he ever blames the ad account.

Selling is math

He doesn't lean on motivation or mindset. Contact 100 people, about 20 pick up, five actually talk, one buys. If you want more sales, you make more contacts. His best salesperson isn't his most talented one. "He's a consistency machine. He calls 100 people every day and he just won't stop." That habit, he says, is what separates people who close every day from people who close once in a while.

Ask questions that make them think

"What's your best lead source?" is a surface question. It gets a surface answer. Yousif goes for questions that pull the prospect toward their own goal and their own problem: How long have you been running without a front desk? How many calls do you think you've missed while you were on a job? What happens if you keep taking calls the way you are now?

He also keeps it light. Prospects who treat the decision as heavy end up "needing to talk to the wife." A little humor, "it's not a disease, give it a try," tells them this is a normal business decision their competitors have already made.

The price of not running ads

When someone says ads are too expensive, he flips the question: do you know the price of not running them? In his own business, the ad budget is one of the smallest lines. Software, AI credits and payroll all cost more. Ads are what keep the rest of it paid for.

Lower their guard by being willing to walk

Buyers have changed. A few years ago his Zoom show rate was around 90% and deals closed fast. Now people want more proof and more reasons to trust you. Sounding needy kills that trust faster than anything.

The story in this episode: a prospect his AI had found showed up in a suit, arms crossed, saying he didn't have time. Yousif told him that if he didn't have time, they probably shouldn't work together. He still showed him everything. By the end the prospect was asking for a deal. Telling people you're there to qualify them, and that not everyone is a fit, does more to drop their guard than any pitch line.

Use their own reason when the price lands

Early in the call, he asks why they really want this. "Between you and I, off the record, what's the reason you're looking for voice AI?" People tell you: more clients, fewer missed calls, looking legit to friends and family. When the price comes up and they start backing out, he goes back to it. You told me you want more clients. If we stop the missed calls, how many more is that a month, and what are they worth?

He also never leads with the company name. Prospects don't care what the company is called. They care what's in it for them.

AI books, people close

Yousif's AI agents book calls and sell his community memberships around the clock. He still says his human salespeople have made him the most money, and they do it by following this training: talk like a person, find the problem, and make enough calls every single day.

title: Stop Buying Leads: Make Them Pay to Become a Lead
summary: From Yousif's Saturday webinar. Why free lead magnets attract people who never buy, how a small paid offer plus a community turns leads into customers who pay attention, how the subscription can cover the ad spend, and how an AI call center follows up with every lead.
content:
This episode comes from a Saturday webinar Yousif Alias ran for business owners already spending real money on ads, which he puts at $500 to $1,000 a month and up. The topic is the funnel he's spent the last three years on: the paid lead magnet, where a lead pays you a small amount before you ever call them.

Why he stopped buying plain leads

Yousif was tired of tire kickers. Leads who ghosted. A month or two with no closed deal after $5,000 or $6,000 in ad spend, and sometimes $10,000 in spend for a single deal. One chargeback or one emergency and the whole thing stopped being sustainable.

He calls the old way "pay up front, chase, and pray." You pay Facebook for a lead, you chase them by phone and text, and you hope they don't need to talk to their wife first. Every month you start back at zero.

The one line to remember

"Get people to pay even one dollar and they'll pay attention to what you're offering a lot better." The amount isn't the point. Paying is what changes how the lead treats you.

Free stuff doesn't get attention anymore

A free PDF, a free consultation ("I hate that word"), five steps to lose belly fat: anyone can get that from ChatGPT in ten seconds, so it carries no value. Free offers fill your list with freebie seekers. Some can't afford what you sell, and the rest won't pay for it. No amount of objection handling fixes that.

What to offer instead

Swap the free lead magnet for a small paid offer, and attach a community to it. AI can write a PDF, but it can't give someone a group of people to belong to. Inside the community you can add perks that fit your business: support, priority booking for a service company, faster shipping if you sell products.

Most of the time, he says, the client already has the right thing and is giving it away. His team renames it, makes it sound more valuable and puts a price on it. Other formats he walks through: a $29 claim for a $500 discount, a $7 or $17 ticket to a webinar, or a monthly community that includes the webinar and the PDF.

A life insurance example

Life insurance agents get plenty of sign-ups, but the leads aren't educated, so they no-show and ghost. Yousif's team changed the funnel so new leads join a $3.99 a month community that teaches them how life insurance works. Those leads pay attention, charge back less, convert better, and some of them end up wanting to join the business as agents.

How the offer pays for the ads

His illustration: say each purchase costs $17 in ads and the community is $7 a month. A member who stays three months has covered what it cost to get them, and you still have the lead. He also showed a real lead from his own account who had paid $184 in subscriptions without ever picking up the phone.

This also changes how you buy ads. With a purchase objective, Meta gets paid when someone buys, the same way e-commerce brands run. For many of the business owners on the webinar, the cost per purchase came in lower than what they were paying per lead.

Follow up with every lead, all day

Some people will opt in and never buy the small offer, so follow-up matters. The second half of the episode is a look at the AI call center his team sets up: one agent tries to close, another tries to book an appointment, and they call at different times through the day until they get an answer. Yousif says his cloned-voice AI setters recently out-booked his human setters. The prompt is built from the methods of top closers, so it handles "I'm not interested" instead of hanging up.

Why now

"What worked two years ago does not work today." People trust companies less and have been burned by high-ticket offers, and they always have options. A paid entry point plus a community gives them a reason to stay with you instead of the next ad they see five minutes later.

title: "I Don't Have the Budget": What That Objection Really Means
summary: A coaching call with a client's sales team after a lost deal. Yousif breaks down why every objection means the prospect doesn't see the value yet, how to acknowledge it, assume the sale and reframe around the money they're missing, and why he records every sales call.
content:
A client's sales team had just lost a deal on a call, and Yousif Alias got on Zoom to coach them through it. This episode is that coaching session. It covers what objections really mean, how to answer them without caving, and why he records every sales call he takes.

Every objection means the same thing

"I don't have the budget." "I need to think about it." "I have to talk to my partner." "Send me the link and I'll pay later." To Yousif these all say one thing: I don't see the value yet. I don't see how this makes me money.

The prospect booked the call and showed up. They wanted something to change. Your job is to bridge where they are now and where they want to be, and your offer is the bridge.

His three steps for any objection

  • 1. Acknowledge it. "I completely understand. I'm the same way."
  • 2. Assume the sale. Ask "debit or credit?" like it's something you do ten times a day.
  • 3. Reframe. Bring them back to the money: two extra deals a month is how much to you?

Do the math with them

In the episode he role-plays it with the team. If the service saves you two deals a month, what is that worth? Once the prospect says a number out loud, the setup price stops looking big next to it. Then you ask how they'd like to pay.

If they say it's too expensive, ask "compared to what?" Most of the time they haven't bought anything like it, so there's nothing to compare. He also takes them to the future: two or three months from now, you'll be asking why we didn't do this sooner.

Hesitating costs you the deal

If you stumble or take forever to ask for the payment, prospects notice. "Even if I have the money, I'm going to say I don't, so I can get out of this." Confidence on the ask matters as much as the offer.

Sending a payment link and hoping rarely works. His closer takes the payment on the call so the deal gets done while the prospect is still there.

Don't lose a deal over price

Yousif admits he used to let deals walk because he wanted full price. Now, when he sees real hesitation on a high-ticket offer, he moves the prospect to a monthly option instead. One client he could have lost over a $4,700 setup fee has since paid about $16,000 in monthly fees. A smaller yes still keeps the business moving.

He also shares how he got started: maxing out a $5,000 Chase card to pay for ads, driving Uber 12 hours a day to pay it off, then maxing it out again the next month.

Take control of the call

Some owners show up wanting to grill you with questions. It doesn't matter if they run a team of a hundred people. Before you answer anything, find out where they stand and what they want. Tell them up front how the call will go: you'll ask a few questions, show them everything, and at the end you'll ask for a yes or no. "If it's a no, I'm a big boy. I won't be hurt." That keeps people from leaving you hanging.

Your setup is your storefront

The backdrop, the books, the camera and the lighting all count. Yousif figures they're 10 to 15% of the close. If you show up in your kitchen, people wonder how you'll handle their business. The rest comes down to what you say.

He also keeps one closer per call. Two salespeople on one prospect feels like a gang-up and makes you look like you're trying too hard. A second person should only join when the closer needs something shown.

Record every call and watch the tape

Yousif records every sales call. He sends the recording to the prospect so the call stays fresh in their mind. When he loses a deal, he watches it back like game film and finds where it went wrong. And when he hires, the recordings become the training. He has hundreds of them going back to 2019, and almost none of those prospects were sure when they got on the call.
